nameStory: The 'parallel-striped' part of this bee's name comes from the distinctive parallel lines that run across its abdomen, like tiny racing stripes. It's called a 'sweat bee' because these small bees are famously attracted to human perspiration, landing on sweaty gardeners and hikers to lap up the salt and moisture.
description: The Parallel-striped Sweat Bee is a small, dark-colored native bee that's commonly seen visiting flowers throughout New England. These bees are typically black or dark metallic green with distinctive light-colored stripes running parallel across their abdomen. They're quite small, usually measuring about a quarter to half an inch long, making them much smaller than honeybees. Like other sweat bees, they're important pollinators that often work quietly alongside more conspicuous bees and butterflies.

idTips.label: Parallel abdominal stripes
idTips.description: Look for clear, light-colored bands that run straight across the dark abdomen like tiny belt stripes - these parallel lines are the bee's signature feature

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than a honeybee, about the size of your pinky fingernail, with a compact, sturdy build

idTips.label: Dark metallic coloration
idTips.description: Body appears black or dark greenish-black with a subtle metallic sheen that catches the light when the bee moves

idTips.label: Attraction to sweat
idTips.description: May land on your arms or hands while gardening, feeling like a tiny, gentle tickle as it seeks salt from your skin

idTips.label: Flower visiting behavior
idTips.description: Often seen working methodically on small flowers, moving deliberately from bloom to bloom rather than hovering like some other bees

habitat: Found in gardens, meadows, forest edges, and anywhere wildflowers bloom throughout New England. They prefer areas with a mix of flowering plants and bare or sparsely vegetated soil where they can dig their nesting burrows. You'll often spot them in suburban gardens, parks, and along sunny woodland trails where diverse flowers provide nectar sources.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from underground nests and begin foraging on early spring flowers. Look for them on dandelions, wild cherries, and other early bloomers.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most commonly seen visiting a wide variety of flowers. This is the best time to observe their distinctive parallel stripes as they work on garden plants and wildflowers.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall as they visit late-season flowers like goldenrod and asters. New generations prepare for winter by going underground.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in underground burrows and are not visible. The bees remain dormant until spring temperatures warm the soil.

funFact: Female Parallel-striped Sweat Bees are tiny construction workers, excavating underground tunnels up to 8 inches deep using nothing but their mandibles and legs - that's like a human digging a tunnel 50 feet deep with their bare hands!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other furrow bees in the same genus, but the Parallel-striped Sweat Bee's evenly spaced, clearly defined abdominal stripes set it apart from the more irregular markings of its relatives. Memory trick: 'Parallel' means the stripes look like they were drawn with a ruler - neat and evenly spaced.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'furrow bee' comes from the shallow grooves or furrows found on the face of bees in the Halictus genus, though these facial features are too small to see without magnification. Don't worry about spotting these furrows in the field - focus on the more visible abdominal stripes instead.
compareHints: Unlike the Ligated Furrow Bee which has more irregular banding, the Parallel-striped Sweat Bee has distinctly even, parallel stripes. It differs from the Orange-legged Furrow Bee by lacking any reddish coloration on the legs. The Confusing Furrow Bee lives up to its name with less distinct markings, making the Parallel-striped's clear stripes a reliable distinguishing feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Ligated Furrow Bee can be distinguished from its close relatives by its consistent dark metallic coloration and widespread abundance — it's the most commonly observed furrow bee in New England with over 6,000 recorded sightings.
Among the furrow bees, orange-legged furrow bees are distinguished by their bright orange legs, while ligated furrow bees have pale legs and more pronounced white abdominal bands.
Compared to the Ligated Furrow Bee, the Confusing Furrow Bee tends to have a more bronze (less greenish) metallic sheen.
